l: Troy, The Library, XII.—TuE Vow or [DOMENEUS
s: Troy was the place of the siege from which Idomeneus was returning when the storm and vow described by Servius occurred.

l: siege of Troy, The Library, XII.—TuE Vow or [DOMENEUS
s: The siege of Troy kept Idomeneus away from Crete while Leucus debauched Meda, murdered her and her daughter, and seized power.

l: Apollodorus, The Library, XII.—TuE Vow or [DOMENEUS
s: Apollodorus says that Leucus debauched Meda, murdered her and her daughter, won ten cities of Crete to his allegiance, and expelled Idomeneus when he returned. He also records the exile story as the source for the first account discussed in the unit.

l: Poseidon, The Library, XII.—TuE Vow or [DOMENEUS
s: Neptune was the deity to whom Idomeneus vowed that he would sacrifice whatever first met him during his return from Troy.

l: Idomeneus's son, The Library, XII.—TuE Vow or [DOMENEUS
s: Idomeneus's son was, according to Servius, the first person to meet Idomeneus after the vow. Idomeneus sacrificed him or attempted to do so; the First Vatican Mythographer instead names a daughter as the victim.

l: Idomeneus's daughter, The Library, XII.—TuE Vow or [DOMENEUS
s: Idomeneus's daughter is identified by the First Vatican Mythographer, rather than his son, as the first person he met and sacrificed or attempted to sacrifice.

l: pestilence, The Library, XII.—TuE Vow or [DOMENEUS
s: A pestilence broke out after Idomeneus sacrificed or attempted to sacrifice his child. The people apparently regarded it as divine judgment for his cruelty.

l: banishment of Idomeneus, The Library, XII.—TuE Vow or [DOMENEUS
s: Idomeneus's banishment followed the pestilence in Servius's account, because the people regarded his treatment of his child as cruel. In Apollodorus's different account, Leucus expelled him after seizing ten cities of Crete.

l: Maeander, The Library, XII.—TuE Vow or [DOMENEUS
s: Maeander, son of Cercaphus and Anaxibia, vowed to the Mother of the Gods that he would sacrifice the first person to congratulate him if he won a war against Pessinus. His son Archelaus, his wife, and his daughter met him, and he sacrificed them before throwing himself into the river that thereafter bore his name.

l: Jephthah, The Library, XII.—TuE Vow or [DOMENEUS
s: Jephthah vowed to the Lord that he would offer as a burnt offering whoever first came out of his house to meet him if he defeated the Ammonites. The unit interprets the vow as intending human sacrifice from the outset.

l: Jephthah's daughter, The Library, XII.—TuE Vow or [DOMENEUS
s: Jephthah's daughter was the first person to meet him after his victory. Jephthah fulfilled his vow by doing to her what he had promised.

l: human sacrifice, The Library, XII.—TuE Vow or [DOMENEUS
s: The unit treats the vows of Maeander and Jephthah as promises of human sacrifice rather than ordinary animal offerings. It also connects them with Idomeneus's sacrifice or attempted sacrifice of his child.

l: German lion-and-daughter folktale, The Library, XII.—TuE Vow or [DOMENEUS
s: In a German story from Hesse, a man promises a lion whatever first meets him at home in exchange for a singing, soaring lark. His youngest daughter meets him first and goes to the lion, who proves to be an enchanted prince and marries her.

l: lion (German folktale), The Library, XII.—TuE Vow or [DOMENEUS
s: The lion threatens to devour a man who tries to take his singing, soaring lark. It accepts the promise of whatever first meets the man at home, but is later revealed to be an enchanted prince who marries the man's daughter.

l: youngest daughter (German folktale), The Library, XII.—TuE Vow or [DOMENEUS
s: The youngest daughter is the man's favourite child and the first person to meet him after he obtains the singing, soaring lark. She bravely agrees to go to the lion, who turns out to be an enchanted prince and becomes her husband.

l: white wolf (Lorraine folktale), The Library, XII.—TuE Vow or [DOMENEUS
s: The white wolf in the Lorraine story owns a castle and its talking roses. It spares a man on condition that he bring the first person he meets at home, receives the man's youngest daughter, and is revealed as a fairy condemned to appear as a wolf by day; after the daughter reveals his secret, he falls dead.

l: youngest daughter (Lorraine folktale), The Library, XII.—TuE Vow or [DOMENEUS
s: The youngest daughter is the first person her father meets after he obtains a talking rose from the white wolf. She willingly goes with him to the castle, where the wolf promises to marry her, but she later reveals his secret and causes him to fall dead.

l: princess (Lithuanian folktale), The Library, XII.—TuE Vow or [DOMENEUS
s: The princess in the Lithuanian story is the youngest and fairest of a king's three daughters. Her father promises her to a white wolf after obtaining a hood of living flowers, and the wolf carries her away before revealing himself as an enchanted prince who eventually marries her.

l: serpent (Tyrolese folktale), The Library, XII.—TuE Vow or [DOMENEUS
s: The serpent in the Tyrolese story demands that a merchant send it the first person he meets at home after he takes a singing and playing leaf. The merchant's youngest daughter goes to it, and it is revealed to be an enchanted nobleman who marries her after the spell is broken.

l: youngest daughter (Tyrolese folktale), The Library, XII.—TuE Vow or [DOMENEUS
s: The youngest daughter asks her father for a leaf that dances, sings, and plays. She is the first person to meet him after he takes one from the serpent's garden, goes willingly to the serpent, and marries it after it becomes a handsome young man.

l: black poodle, The Library, XII.—TuE Vow or [DOMENEUS
s: The black poodle promises a king a tinkling lion-leaf in exchange for whatever first comes out of the king's house to meet him. It carries off the king's youngest daughter after she is identified as the promised person, but is revealed to be an enchanted prince when she burns its dog-skin.

l: The Library, The Library, Two stories of the same general type have been recorded in
s: Two stories of the same general type were recorded in Schleswig-Holstein. In the first, a king promises a big bear whatever first meets him at his castle in exchange for a golden jingle-jangle, and his youngest daughter becomes bound to the promise. The bear is transformed into a rich and handsome prince after the daughter treads on his paw, and he marries her. In the second, a king promises a little black man whatever first comes out of his house, and his daughter is taken away by a white wolf who turns out to be an enchanted prince.

l: Schleswig-Holstein, The Library, Two stories of the same general type have been recorded in
s: Two stories of the same general type were recorded there.

l: first Schleswig-Holstein story, The Library, Two stories of the same general type have been recorded in
s: It concerns a king who promises a big bear whatever first meets him at his castle in exchange for a golden jingle-jangle. The king's youngest daughter is eventually sent to the bear, who is transformed into a rich and handsome prince and marries her.

l: king (first Schleswig-Holstein story), The Library, Two stories of the same general type have been recorded in
s: He has three daughters and promises the big bear whatever first meets him at his castle in exchange for a golden jingle-jangle. He tries to substitute the shepherd's daughter and the swineherd's daughter for his youngest daughter, but ultimately sends the youngest daughter to the bear.

l: youngest daughter (first Schleswig-Holstein story), The Library, Two stories of the same general type have been recorded in
s: She is the first person to meet the big bear at the castle, and her father eventually sends her to him. She later visits her father's castle with the bear, treads heavily on one of his paws, and becomes the wife of the prince into whom he is transformed.

l: big bear (first Schleswig-Holstein story), The Library, Two stories of the same general type have been recorded in
s: He watches over the golden jingle-jangles on a great tall tree and agrees to give one to the king in exchange for whatever first meets the king at his castle. He rejects substitutes sent by the king, accepts the youngest daughter, and is changed into a rich and handsome prince when she treads on his paw.

l: prince (first Schleswig-Holstein story), The Library, Two stories of the same general type have been recorded in
s: He is the rich and handsome form assumed by the big bear after the youngest daughter treads on one of his paws. He takes the daughter to wife.

l: golden jingle-jangle, The Library, Two stories of the same general type have been recorded in
s: It is the youngest daughter's requested present. A big bear gives one to the king in exchange for whatever first meets him at his castle.

l: second Schleswig-Holstein story, The Library, Two stories of the same general type have been recorded in
s: It concerns a king who promises a little black man whatever first comes out of his house to meet him. His daughter is the first to appear and is taken away by a white wolf, who turns out to be an enchanted prince.

l: little black man, The Library, Two stories of the same general type have been recorded in
s: He appears to a king who has lost his way and offers to guide him home if the king promises to give him whatever first comes out of the king's house to meet him.

l: daughter (second Schleswig-Holstein story), The Library, Two stories of the same general type have been recorded in
s: She is the first to run out of the king's house when he returns. She willingly goes away after learning that she has been promised, and a white wolf fetches her.

l: white wolf, The Library, Two stories of the same general type have been recorded in
s: He fetches the king's daughter after she becomes bound by the king's promise. He turns out to be an enchanted prince and marries her when the spell binding him is broken.

l: enchanted prince (second Schleswig-Holstein story), The Library, Two stories of the same general type have been recorded in
s: He is the form revealed by the white wolf after the spell binding him is broken. He marries the king's daughter.

l: nobleman (German story), The Library, Two stories of the same general type have been recorded in
s: He loses his way in a wood and meets a poodle that offers to guide him home in exchange for whatever first comes out of his house to meet him. His daughter is the first to appear, and the apparent calamity ends in her marriage with a prince.

l: poodle, The Library, Two stories of the same general type have been recorded in
s: It meets a nobleman who has lost his way and offers to guide him home if he will give it whatever first comes out of his house to meet him.

l: youngest daughter (Swedish story), The Library, Two stories of the same general type have been recorded in
s: She is the king's youngest and dearest daughter and is the first living thing to meet him when he returns home. Her father eventually sends her into the forest, and she is happily wedded to the man in the grey cloak.

l: man in the grey cloak, The Library, Two stories of the same general type have been recorded in
s: He repeatedly meets a king who is lost in the forest and says that the king must give him the first living thing that meets him at home. He sends the king's two elder daughters back with rich presents and later becomes the husband of the youngest daughter.

l: enchanted prince or nobleman (Swedish story), The Library, Two stories of the same general type have been recorded in
s: The man in the grey cloak turns out to be an enchanted prince or nobleman. He owns a fine castle and happily marries the youngest daughter.

l: rash vow, The Library, Two stories of the same general type have been recorded in
s: In these folk-tales, it generally turns out fortunately for the person bound by it, who obtains a princely husband and wedded bliss.

l: vow, The Library, Two stories of the same general type have been recorded in
s: The stories involve promises to give a supernatural or animal figure whatever first meets or comes out to greet a returning man. The text suggests that such vows may preserve a reminiscence of a custom that in real life could end in sacrifice.

l: sacrifice of the victim, The Library, Two stories of the same general type have been recorded in
s: The text contrasts the happy endings of the folk-tales with the possibility that the promised victim was sacrificed or killed in real life.

l: custom of sacrificial vows, The Library, Two stories of the same general type have been recorded in
s: The stories are said to preserve a possible reminiscence of a custom in which a vow could end with the sacrifice of the victim at the altar.

l: Idomeneus, The Library, Two stories of the same general type have been recorded in
s: His legends are cited as seeming to preserve a record of a custom involving sacrificial vows.

l: The Library, The Library, XIII.—Untyssts AND PoLYPHEMUS
s: This unit examines the widespread Ulysses and Polyphemus story and compares the Homeric account with later oral and literary versions. It focuses especially on John of Haute-Seille's Dolopathos, which preserves a version in which a famous robber encounters a giant, blinds him with boiling oil, escapes disguised among sheep, and loses a finger because of a magic ring. The Dolopathos version differs from the Odyssey by making the giant blear-eyed rather than one-eyed, having the blinding occur through a trick with the giant's consent, and adding the magic-ring episode. These differences are presented as evidence that John drew on oral tradition rather than directly on the Odyssey.

l: Ulysses, The Library, XIII.—Untyssts AND PoLYPHEMUS
s: Ulysses is the hero associated with the story of Polyphemus. In Dolopathos, the giant's antagonist is represented instead by a famous robber, while the text notes that John of Haute-Seille knew of Ulysses, Circe, and Polyphemus.

l: Polyphemus, The Library, XIII.—Untyssts AND PoLYPHEMUS
s: Polyphemus is the giant associated with the story. The Dolopathos version mentions him by name in its surrounding discussion, but its narrative presents the giant as blear-eyed rather than one-eyed and includes episodes differing from the Odyssey.

l: Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus, The Library, XIII.—Untyssts AND PoLYPHEMUS
s: The story has been recorded in modern times among many widely separated peoples, whose versions resemble one another closely. Its common source may have been the Odyssey or, more probably, an older folk-tale incorporated by Homer.

l: The Odyssey, The Library, XIII.—Untyssts AND PoLYPHEMUS
s: The Odyssey contains the well-known account of Ulysses and Polyphemus. The Dolopathos narrative differs from it in the giant's condition, the method of blinding, and the addition of the magic-ring episode.

l: John of Haute-Seille, The Library, XIII.—Untyssts AND PoLYPHEMUS
s: John of Haute-Seille was a monk of the Cistercian Abbey of Haute-Seille in Lorraine who wrote Dolopathos in or soon after 1184. He appears to have known the Odyssey, but his account of Polyphemus is inferred to have followed oral tradition rather than the Homeric narrative.

l: Dolopathos sive de Rege et Septem Sapientibus, The Library, XIII.—Untyssts AND PoLYPHEMUS
s: Dolopathos is a mediaeval collection of tales written in Latin by John of Haute-Seille. It contains a version of the Polyphemus story in which a famous robber defeats a giant through deception, and its account diverges in notable ways from the Odyssey.

l: famous robber (Dolopathos), The Library, XIII.—Untyssts AND PoLYPHEMUS
s: The famous robber had accumulated great riches through robbery before resolving in old age to practice virtue. He recounts that he and other robbers were captured by a giant, that he blinded the giant with a harmful boiling salve, escaped among the sheep, and finally cut off a finger bearing the giant's magic ring.

l: the hundred robbers, The Library, XIII.—Untyssts AND PoLYPHEMUS
s: The hundred robbers went to the giant's dwelling to steal his gold and silver while he was absent. The giant and nine others captured them, divided them among themselves, and the famous robber and nine companions were taken to the giant whose wealth they had stolen.

l: giant's cave, The Library, XIII.—Untyssts AND PoLYPHEMUS
s: The giant's cave was the robbers' prison and was strongly enclosed by masonry, with an iron-barred door as its only exit. The famous robber escaped from it by hiding among the giant's sheep and passing through the doorway with the flock.

l: magic ring (giant's ring), The Library, XIII.—Untyssts AND PoLYPHEMUS
s: After the robber escaped, the blind giant offered him a gold ring as a guest's reward. The ring bewitched the robber, forcing him to shout that he was there; he cut off the finger bearing it and threw the finger and ring to the giant in order to escape.

l: the giant's blinding, The Library, XIII.—Untyssts AND PoLYPHEMUS
s: The giant's blinding was achieved after the robber pretended to be a doctor and promised to cure his aching eyes. The robber poured boiling oil mixed with lime, salt, sulphur, arsenic, and other harmful substances over the giant's head, leaving him completely blind.

l: the hero's escape from the giant, The Library, XIII.—Untyssts AND PoLYPHEMUS
s: The hero first hid from the blinded giant by climbing to the roof and hanging from a beam. He then disguised himself in a ram's fleece, passed among the flock while the giant counted the sheep, and was driven outside; the magic ring afterward forced him to sacrifice a finger before he could escape completely.

l: oral tradition, The Library, XIII.—Untyssts AND PoLYPHEMUS
s: Oral tradition is presented as the likely source of the unusual features in the Dolopathos version. The recurrence of those features in popular versions supports the view that John of Haute-Seille drew on oral tradition rather than solely on the Odyssey.

l: The Library, The Library, (2) All the distinctive features which we have just remarked
s: The unit compares several Celtic, Basque, Rumanian, and Italian versions of the Ulysses and Polyphemus story. In the Islay tale, Conall Cra Bhuidhe blinds a one-eyed giant, escapes from his cave disguised in a buck’s skin, and defeats the giant with a talking ring and a severed finger. Related Basque and Rumanian stories likewise feature a one-eyed giant, escape through a sheep or ram disguise, a talking ring, and the severing of the hero’s finger. An Italian story includes the same general pattern, but its ring is enchanted rather than talking.

l: Conall Cra Bhuidhe, The Library, (2) All the distinctive features which we have just remarked
s: Conall Cra Bhuidhe tries to steal the brown horse of the King of Lochlann with his sons. After being caught, he saves their lives by telling of his adventures, including how he blinded a one-eyed giant, escaped in a buck’s skin, and defeated the giant with a ring and a severed finger.

l: King of Lochlann, The Library, (2) All the distinctive features which we have just remarked
s: The King of Lochlann catches Conall Cra Bhuidhe and his sons while they are attempting to steal his brown horse. He would have hanged them, but Conall saves their lives by telling his story.

l: Conall's giant, The Library, (2) All the distinctive features which we have just remarked
s: Conall’s giant is a one-eyed giant who keeps goats in a cave and intends to eat Conall. Conall blinds him by pretending to restore his sight in a cauldron, escapes in the buck’s skin, and causes him to drown while pursuing a ring.

l: Conall's goats, The Library, (2) All the distinctive features which we have just remarked
s: Conall’s goats are kept by the giant and are released one by one while the giant, unable to see, feels them at the cave’s entrance. Conall uses the release of the goats to escape while disguised in the buck’s skin.

l: Conall's buck, The Library, (2) All the distinctive features which we have just remarked
s: Conall’s buck is at the head of the giant’s goats. Conall kills it, flays it bag-wise, and uses its skin and position to pass the giant at the cave entrance.

l: talking ring (Conall's giant's ring), The Library, (2) All the distinctive features which we have just remarked
s: The giant gives Conall a ring that answers when the giant asks where it is. Conall cuts off the finger bearing the ring and throws it into deep water; the giant follows the ring’s voice into the water and drowns.

l: Ulysses, The Library, (2) All the distinctive features which we have just remarked
s: Ulysses is mentioned as the comparable hero in the cave episode of the story. The unit does not otherwise describe his actions.

l: Polyphemus, The Library, (2) All the distinctive features which we have just remarked
s: Polyphemus is mentioned as the comparable one-eyed cave giant in the story. The unit does not otherwise describe his actions.

l: Tartaro, The Library, (2) All the distinctive features which we have just remarked
s: Tartaro is a one-eyed colossus who shepherds and hunts people and eats a sheep before his human victims. A young man blinds him, escapes disguised in a sheep’s skin, and defeats his pursuit after cutting off the finger bearing Tartaro’s ring.

l: young man (Tartaro story), The Library, (2) All the distinctive features which we have just remarked
s: The young man is captured by Tartaro and realizes that he must escape after seeing the giant eat a sheep. He blinds Tartaro with a red-hot spit, escapes through the flock in a sheep’s skin, and cuts off his own finger to get rid of the ring that reveals his location.

l: Tartaro's ring, The Library, (2) All the distinctive features which we have just remarked
s: Tartaro’s ring is given to the escaping young man as a supposed remembrance of his escape. It cries out that the young man has it, so he cuts off the finger bearing it and throws it away.

l: Basa-Jaun, The Library, (2) All the distinctive features which we have just remarked
s: Basa-Jaun is a hairy, one-eyed giant who eats one of two soldiers and tries to catch the other. The surviving soldier blinds him, escapes in a sheep’s skin, and causes him to drown after cutting off the finger bearing Basa-Jaun’s talking ring.

l: soldier (Basa-Jaun story), The Library, (2) All the distinctive features which we have just remarked
s: The soldier survives after Basa-Jaun eats his companion. He blinds Basa-Jaun with a heated spit, escapes among the sheep in a sheep’s skin, and cuts off his finger to throw away the ring that is calling out his location.

l: Rumanian giant, The Library, (2) All the distinctive features which we have just remarked
s: The Rumanian giant captures three brothers, eats the eldest and second brother, and tries to catch the youngest. After being blinded, he pursues the youngest because a ring reveals the youth’s location, but he drowns when the severed finger and ring are thrown into the water.

l: three brothers, The Library, (2) All the distinctive features which we have just remarked
s: The three brothers are taken by the Rumanian giant after answering his calls at night. The eldest and second brothers are eaten, while the youngest survives and escapes.

l: youngest brother, The Library, (2) All the distinctive features which we have just remarked
s: The youngest brother survives after the Rumanian giant eats his two brothers. He blinds the giant, escapes disguised in a ram’s skin, and cuts off his finger to throw the talking ring into the water, causing the giant to drown.

l: Italian Eye-in-his-forehead, The Library, (2) All the distinctive features which we have just remarked
s: Italian Eye-in-his-forehead is a one-eyed giant who eats Big Brother and plans to eat Little Brother. Little Brother blinds him, escapes in a ram’s skin, and cuts off the finger bearing the enchanted ring when it forces him toward the giant.

l: Big Brother, The Library, (2) All the distinctive features which we have just remarked
s: Big Brother is chosen by lot to be eaten first by Italian Eye-in-his-forehead. The giant roasts him on a spit and eats him.

l: Little Brother, The Library, (2) All the distinctive features which we have just remarked
s: Little Brother escapes Italian Eye-in-his-forehead after pretending to eat Big Brother, blinding the giant, and disguising himself in a ram’s skin. He cuts off the finger bearing the enchanted ring and throws it at the giant.

l: John of Haute-Seille's version, The Library, (2) All the distinctive features which we have just remarked
s: John of Haute-Seille’s version is identified as having distinctive features that recur in the West Highland story and related versions. The unit does not separately recount its plot.

l: Ulysses and Polyphemus, The Library, (2) All the distinctive features which we have just remarked
s: Ulysses and Polyphemus is the story pattern to which the unit’s West Highland, Basque, Rumanian, and Italian tales are compared. Its recurring features include a one-eyed giant, blinding, escape among sheep or goats, and in several versions a ring that leads to the giant’s death.

l: The Library, The Library, (8) Another Italian version of the story, recorded at Pisa,
s: The Italian story concerns a man of Florence, a curate, and a workman who enter the house of a giant seeking employment. The giant kills the curate and workman, but the man of Florence blinds him with boiling oil, escapes after cutting off a finger trapped by a magical ring, and returns to Florence. The Serbian story concerns a priest and his scholar, who encounter a one-eyed giant in a cave. The giant roasts the priest, but the scholar blinds him, escapes disguised in a ram’s skin, and cuts off a finger trapped by a staff.

l: man of Florence, The Library, (8) Another Italian version of the story, recorded at Pisa,
s: The man of Florence travels with a curate and a workman and accepts employment at a giant’s house. He discovers that the giant kills his workers, blinds the giant with boiling oil, escapes after cutting off a finger trapped by a ring, and returns exhausted to Florence, where he no longer wishes to travel and recount his adventures.

l: curate, The Library, (8) Another Italian version of the story, recorded at Pisa,
s: The curate accepts a position in the giant’s parish. When the giant shows him some leaves, the giant cuts off his head with a scimitar and buries his body in a chamber.

l: workman, The Library, (8) Another Italian version of the story, recorded at Pisa,
s: The workman accepts a position in the giant’s workshop. The giant shows him some leaves and then cuts off his head with a scimitar in the same chamber.

l: giant in the Italian story, The Library, (8) Another Italian version of the story, recorded at Pisa,
s: The giant offers employment to the man of Florence, the curate, and the workman, but kills the curate and workman while pretending to give them their jobs. The man of Florence blinds him with boiling oil, and the giant pursues him while carrying a marble table and later gives him a ring that turns his finger to marble.

l: boiling oil treatment, The Library, (8) Another Italian version of the story, recorded at Pisa,
s: The man of Florence claims that a herb boiled in oil will cure the giant’s defective eye. He ties the giant to a marble table and pours the boiling oil over both of the giant’s eyes, blinding him.

l: escape from the giant, The Library, (8) Another Italian version of the story, recorded at Pisa,
s: The man of Florence escapes after blinding the giant, but a ring thrown by the giant turns his finger to marble and prevents him from moving. He cuts off the finger with a knife and escapes while the giant, burdened by the marble table, cannot catch him.

l: Serbian priest, The Library, (8) Another Italian version of the story, recorded at Pisa,
s: The Serbian priest travels through a mountainous region with his scholar and enters a cave occupied by a one-eyed giant. The giant judges him to be the fatter of the two travellers, kills him, and roasts him over the fire.

l: Serbian scholar, The Library, (8) Another Italian version of the story, recorded at Pisa,
s: The Serbian scholar travels with the priest and is forced by the giant to take a mouthful of the roasted priest’s flesh, which he secretly spits out. He blinds the sleeping giant with a sharpened stick, escapes in a ram’s skin among the sheep, and cuts off a finger trapped by the giant’s staff.

l: cave, The Library, (8) Another Italian version of the story, recorded at Pisa,
s: The cave contains a one-eyed giant, a great fire, and many sheep. Its entrance is blocked by a huge stone that the giant can lift, and the scholar escapes from it disguised in a ram’s skin.

l: one-eyed giant in the Serbian story, The Library, (8) Another Italian version of the story, recorded at Pisa,
s: The one-eyed giant lets the priest and scholar into the cave, blocks the entrance with a huge stone, and roasts the priest. The scholar blinds him with a sharpened stick and escapes, while the giant later pursues him and falls into the water.

l: roasted parson, The Library, (8) Another Italian version of the story, recorded at Pisa,
s: The roasted parson is the Serbian priest, whom the one-eyed giant selects as the fatter traveller. The giant knocks him on the head, places him on a spit, roasts him, and forces the scholar to taste the flesh.

l: sheep, The Library, (8) Another Italian version of the story, recorded at Pisa,
s: The sheep are in the cave with the one-eyed giant. The scholar hides among them while wearing a ram’s skin and slips out when the giant releases the sheep one by one.

l: ram’s skin disguise, The Library, (8) Another Italian version of the story, recorded at Pisa,
s: The Serbian scholar draws a ram’s skin over his body and mingles with the sheep in the cave. The disguise enables him to pass through the cave entrance and escape from the giant.

l: The Library, The Library, (10) A Russian story, which belongs to the same class,
s: The Russian story tells of a smith who seeks evil, meets Likho in the form of a one-eyed woman, and escapes after tricking and injuring her, though he loses a hand to a golden-handled hatchet. The Esthonian story similarly has a Barn-carl blind the devil with molten lead after calling himself “Myself,” a trick compared with Ulysses’ use of “Nobody” against Polyphemus. In a Lapp tale, four Lapps encounter a giant in his cave, blind him with molten lead, and escape in goat skins while carrying away treasure. A related Lapp variant describes Slyboots blinding the Stalo with molten lead and escaping from his sheepfold in a ram’s skin.

l: Russian story, The Library, (10) A Russian story, which belongs to the same class,
s: The Russian story concerns a smith who searches for evil, encounters Likho, and escapes by disguising himself as a sheep. It is said to belong to the same class as related stories from Esthonia and Lapland.

l: smith, The Library, (10) A Russian story, which belongs to the same class,
s: The smith sets out to seek evil and meets a tailor who joins him. At Likho’s cottage, he tricks the one-eyed woman into being tied up, attacks her eye, escapes disguised as a sheep, and later cuts off his own hand when it becomes stuck to a golden-handled hatchet.

l: tailor, The Library, (10) A Russian story, which belongs to the same class,
s: The tailor joins the smith in searching for evil. The one-eyed woman cuts his throat, trusses him, and puts him in the oven.

l: Likho, The Library, (10) A Russian story, which belongs to the same class,
s: Likho is identified with evil in the Russian story and appears as a tall, crooked, one-eyed woman. She pursues the smith after he escapes and causes his hand to stick to a golden-handled hatchet.

l: one-eyed woman (Likho's cottage), The Library, (10) A Russian story, which belongs to the same class,
s: The one-eyed woman lives in a large, bare, squalid cottage in a dark forest. She kills the tailor, tries to attack the smith, and is tricked when the smith pretends to be a sheep.

l: Esthonian story, The Library, (10) A Russian story, which belongs to the same class,
s: The Esthonian story concerns a Barn-carl who tricks the devil by pretending to cast eyes. Its use of the name “Myself” is said to resemble Ulysses’ use of “Nobody” against Polyphemus.

l: Barn-carl, The Library, (10) A Russian story, which belongs to the same class,
s: The Barn-carl, a farm-servant responsible for barns and corn, tells the devil that he casts eyes. He binds the devil, pours molten lead on his eyes, and escapes the consequences by saying that “Myself” did it.

l: devil, The Library, (10) A Russian story, which belongs to the same class,
s: The devil asks the Barn-carl to make him a new pair of eyes. After being bound and blinded with molten lead, he runs past some ploughmen, claims that “Myself” injured him, and later dies of his new eyes.

l: Myself, The Library, (10) A Russian story, which belongs to the same class,
s: “Myself” is the name the Barn-carl gives when the devil asks who he is. The name allows the Barn-carl to answer truthfully that “Myself” blinded the devil.

l: Ulysses, The Library, (10) A Russian story, which belongs to the same class,
s: Ulysses is mentioned as using the trick of calling himself “Nobody” against Polyphemus. This trick is compared with the Barn-carl’s use of “Myself.”

l: Polyphemus, The Library, (10) A Russian story, which belongs to the same class,
s: Polyphemus is mentioned as the figure against whom Ulysses plays the trick of calling himself “Nobody.” The text compares this trick with similar tricks in the Esthonian and Lapp stories.

l: Lapp tale, The Library, (10) A Russian story, which belongs to the same class,
s: The Lapp tale concerns four Lapps who enter a giant’s cave, blind the giant with molten lead, and escape disguised in goat skins. It resembles the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus more closely than the Russian and Esthonian stories do.

l: Lapps, The Library, (10) A Russian story, which belongs to the same class,
s: Four Lapps lose their way, enter a giant’s cave, and hide after eating his beef. They blind the giant with molten lead, escape in the skins of billy-goats with gold and silver, and leave the giant unable to find them.

l: giant, The Library, (10) A Russian story, which belongs to the same class,
s: The giant owns a cave, goats, and great riches, and captures the Lapps after discovering them inside. The Lapps trick him into accepting molten lead as eye-salve, blind him, and escape while disguised as goats.

l: giant's cave, The Library, (10) A Russian story, which belongs to the same class,
s: The giant’s cave has silver walls and a roof, a large hearth, a kettle, more than a hundred goats, and stores of gold and silver. The Lapps hide there, blind the giant, and escape through its entrance in goat skins.

l: Nobody, The Library, (10) A Russian story, which belongs to the same class,
s: “Nobody” is the name one Lapp gives the giant when asked to identify himself. After the Lapp blinds the giant, the giant’s neighbor refuses to help because the giant says that Nobody hurt him.

l: Lapp variant, The Library, (10) A Russian story, which belongs to the same class,
s: The Lapp variant concerns Slyboots and a Stalo who tries to fatten him before eating him. It repeats the blinding trick and ends with Slyboots escaping from the sheepfold in the skin of a ram.

l: Slyboots, The Library, (10) A Russian story, which belongs to the same class,
s: Slyboots persuades the Stalo that molten lead will make him sharp-sighted, then pours it into both of the Stalo’s eyes. He cooks the Stalo’s dog for him, releases the sheep, disguises himself in the big ram’s skin, and crawls out of the fold.

l: Stalo, The Library, (10) A Russian story, which belongs to the same class,
s: The Stalo owns a house, a kitchen, and sheep, and keeps Lapps so that he can fatten and eat them. Slyboots blinds him with molten lead, deceives him with dog meat, and escapes past him in a ram’s skin.

l: Stalo's sheep, The Library, (10) A Russian story, which belongs to the same class,
s: The Stalo’s sheep are kept in a fold and are released one by one. Slyboots kills and skins the big ram, then uses its skin to disguise himself while escaping.

l: Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus, The Library, (10) A Russian story, which belongs to the same class,
s: The Ulysses and Polyphemus story is used as a comparison for the tricks involving the names “Nobody” and “Myself.” The Lapp tale is said to resemble it especially closely.

l: The Library, The Library, (14) A Finnish tale of the same general type, but lacking
s: The unit presents Finnish, Karelian, Lithuanian, German, Yorkshire, and Breton versions of the Ulysses and Polyphemus story. In the Finnish tale, Gylpho rescues imprisoned princesses by blinding and killing the one-eyed rock-spirit Kammo. In the Lithuanian tale, a skipper and his crew blind an island giant and escape beneath sheep, while similar escapes occur in the German, Yorkshire, and Breton versions. The second Breton tale follows Bihanic as he steals a giant’s treasures, including an oracular parrot, and escapes after killing the giantess cook.

l: Finnish tale, The Library, (14) A Finnish tale of the same general type, but lacking
s: The Finnish tale concerns the poor ostler Gylpho, who attempts to free three spellbound king’s daughters from an underground cave. It includes a one-eyed rock-spirit who is blinded with a heated poker.

l: Gylpho, The Library, (14) A Finnish tale of the same general type, but lacking
s: Gylpho sets out to free three imprisoned princesses. He heats an iron poker red-hot, thrusts it into Kammo’s eye, and then hews off the spirit’s head.

l: Kammo, The Library, (14) A Finnish tale of the same general type, but lacking
s: Kammo is an old rock-spirit with a great horn and one eye in the middle of his forehead. His dim eye is blinded by Gylpho with a red-hot poker, after which Gylpho cuts off his head.

l: Ulysses, The Library, (14) A Finnish tale of the same general type, but lacking
s: Ulysses is mentioned as the Greek hero whose story provides the general type for the tales in this unit. The Karelian hero and others use stratagems like those attributed to Ulysses.

l: Polyphemus, The Library, (14) A Finnish tale of the same general type, but lacking
s: Polyphemus is mentioned in connection with the Homeric story that the Finnish, Karelian, Lithuanian, German, Yorkshire, and Breton tales resemble.

l: one-eyed giant, The Library, (14) A Finnish tale of the same general type, but lacking
s: The one-eyed giant in the Karelian story guards a castle and is blinded at night by the hero. The hero then hides under a sheep and escapes when the giant sends the flock out to graze.

l: Lithuanian tale, The Library, (14) A Finnish tale of the same general type, but lacking
s: The Lithuanian tale tells of sailors who enter a giant’s underground house after lifting a stone covering its entrance. They blind the giant with a heated iron spit and escape under sheep, though the giant’s thrown rocks damage their ship and kill some crew members.

l: skipper, The Library, (14) A Finnish tale of the same general type, but lacking
s: The skipper lands on the island with his crew and devises their escape from the giant. He heats an iron spit, helps ram it into the giant’s eye, and later hides under the old tup to leave with the sheep.

l: ship’s crew, The Library, (14) A Finnish tale of the same general type, but lacking
s: The ship’s crew enters the giant’s cave and loses one member when the giant swallows him. The surviving crew helps blind the giant and escapes under the sheep, but some members are killed when a rock strikes the ship.

l: giant of the island, The Library, (14) A Finnish tale of the same general type, but lacking
s: The giant of the island has one eye in the middle of his forehead and lives in a huge cave beneath a mountain. He swallows one sailor, is blinded by a heated spit, and later throws rocks at the departing ship.

l: sheep flock, The Library, (14) A Finnish tale of the same general type, but lacking
s: The sheep flock belongs to the island giant and provides the sailors with a means of escape. The sailors tie themselves beneath the sheep and pass out of the cave when the flock leaves.

l: Yorkshire giant, The Library, (14) A Finnish tale of the same general type, but lacking
s: The Yorkshire giant lives at a mill, grinds men’s bones to make bread, and has one eye. Jack blinds him with a knife and escapes by disguising himself in the hide of the giant’s dog.

l: Jack, The Library, (14) A Finnish tale of the same general type, but lacking
s: Jack serves the Yorkshire giant for many years and eventually decides to leave for Topcliffe Fair. He takes the giant’s knife, thrusts it into the giant’s single eye, kills the giant’s dog, and escapes under its hide.

l: Breton version, The Library, (14) A Finnish tale of the same general type, but lacking
s: One Breton version tells of a young man who blinds a one-eyed giant with a pistol and escapes beneath a sheep. Another Breton version concerns Bihanic, who steals a giant’s treasures and escapes after killing the giantess cook.

l: young man, The Library, (14) A Finnish tale of the same general type, but lacking
s: The young man in the Breton version encounters a one-eyed giant who keeps human flesh in his hut. He shoots out the giant’s eye, hides among the sheep, and escapes beneath one of them before selling the sheep in the market.

l: Bihanic, The Library, (14) A Finnish tale of the same general type, but lacking
s: Bihanic is the youngest of three brothers and is sent by a king to rob a giant of his treasures. After entering the castle disguised in a sheep’s skin, he kills the giantess cook, takes the oracular parrot, and flees.

l: giant’s treasures, The Library, (14) A Finnish tale of the same general type, but lacking
s: The giant’s treasures consist of an oracular parrot, a swift dromedary, and a carbuncle whose light illuminates the night for seven leagues. Bihanic obtains the dromedary and carbuncle relatively easily and later steals the parrot.

l: oracular parrot, The Library, (14) A Finnish tale of the same general type, but lacking
s: The oracular parrot possesses the gift of second sight and is consulted by the giant morning and evening. It identifies Bihanic as the giant’s enemy and reveals that he is hiding in the sheepfold, but Bihanic ultimately captures it.

l: The Library, The Library, (21) A Gascon version of the old heathen tale is enriched
s: A poor widow's boy and girl travel to the land of the Ogres to gather golden horns and become wealthy. An Ogre captures them, roasts and swallows the girl, and threatens to eat the boy, but the boy blinds him with a burning brand. The boy escapes the cave disguised among the sheep, and the Ogre later vomits up the girl alive. The brother and sister return to their mother with great riches.

l: poor widow, The Library, (21) A Gascon version of the old heathen tale is enriched
s: The poor widow lives in a cottage with her boy and girl. She warns the boy about the dangers of the land of the Ogres but finally consents to the children's journey and gives the girl a little silver cross.

l: boy, The Library, (21) A Gascon version of the old heathen tale is enriched
s: The boy decides to seek his fortune by gathering golden horns in the land of the Ogres. After an Ogre captures him and his sister, he talks to delay his fate, blinds the Ogre with a glowing brand, disguises himself in a sheep's skin and golden horns, and escapes the cave.

l: girl, The Library, (21) A Gascon version of the old heathen tale is enriched
s: The girl goes with her brother to guard him and carries the little silver cross. The Ogre roasts her alive and swallows her, but he later vomits her up alive, allowing her to return with her brother to their mother.

l: giants, The Library, (21) A Gascon version of the old heathen tale is enriched
s: The Ogres are giants seven fathoms tall with one eye in the middle of the forehead. They tend oxen and sheep with golden horns, roast captured Christians on gridirons, and live in caves in a wild black country.

l: Christians, The Library, (21) A Gascon version of the old heathen tale is enriched
s: The Ogres capture and eat Christians. The boy and girl are called little Christians by the Ogre, and the boy says that Christians do not eat one another.

l: land of the Ogres, The Library, (21) A Gascon version of the old heathen tale is enriched
s: The land of the Ogres lies far from the children's home towards the setting sun. It has high mountains, waterfalls, no priests, churches, or churchyards, and contains oxen and sheep with golden horns.

l: wild black country, The Library, (21) A Gascon version of the old heathen tale is enriched
s: The wild black country is a mountainous region where streams fall from heights of three thousand feet. The Ogres live there, and it has no priests, churches, or churchyards.

l: cave (the Ogre's cave), The Library, (21) A Gascon version of the old heathen tale is enriched
s: The Ogre's cave is closed by a massive stone and contains the Ogre, the children, and cattle with golden horns. The boy hides there, blinds the Ogre, waits three days and nights, and escapes when the entrance is opened for the hungry cattle.

l: silver cross, The Library, (21) A Gascon version of the old heathen tale is enriched
s: The poor widow gives the girl a little silver cross and tells her never to part with it. The girl holds it while she prays as she is roasted alive.

l: golden horns, The Library, (21) A Gascon version of the old heathen tale is enriched
s: The golden horns come from the Ogres' oxen and sheep, whose discarded horns the children collect. The children gather a hundred golden horns and return with great riches; the boy also uses a sheep's golden horns as part of his disguise.

l: gridiron, The Library, (21) A Gascon version of the old heathen tale is enriched
s: The Ogres use a gridiron to roast captured Christians. The girl is laid on one and roasted alive over a slow fire.

l: flat stone (the cave entrance stone), The Library, (21) A Gascon version of the old heathen tale is enriched
s: The cave entrance is blocked by a flat stone weighing a hundred hundredweights. The Ogre moves it with his shoulder, and later the boy cannot move it; the stone finally falls when the Ogre opens the cave for the cattle.

l: journey to the land of the Ogres, The Library, (21) A Gascon version of the old heathen tale is enriched
s: The boy and girl travel towards the setting sun for seven months. They live on alms and sleep in the stables of charitable people before reaching the land of the Ogres.

l: search for golden horns, The Library, (21) A Gascon version of the old heathen tale is enriched
s: For seven days the boy and girl search the mountains for golden horns while hiding under bushes and among rocks. Their wallets become full with a hundred horns before they decide to return home.

l: capture of the children, The Library, (21) A Gascon version of the old heathen tale is enriched
s: An Ogre sees the children while driving his oxen and sheep and throws them into a big bag. He carries them to his cave and orders them to turn the spit while he prepares a meal.

l: roasting of the girl, The Library, (21) A Gascon version of the old heathen tale is enriched
s: The Ogre becomes enraged when the girl begins to pray to God. He strips her, lays her on a gridiron, and roasts her alive before swallowing her in one mouthful.

l: blinding of the Ogre, The Library, (21) A Gascon version of the old heathen tale is enriched
s: After the Ogre falls asleep, the boy takes a glowing brand from the hearth and thrusts it into the Ogre's eye. The Ogre becomes blind and cries out that he is blind.

l: escape from the cave, The Library, (21) A Gascon version of the old heathen tale is enriched
s: The boy hides among the cattle and later disguises himself with a sheep's skin and golden horns. He passes among the sheep as the blind Ogre counts them, then runs away when the Ogre suspects him.

l: vomiting up the girl, The Library, (21) A Gascon version of the old heathen tale is enriched
s: The Ogre becomes sick and vomits up the girl alive after swallowing her. This allows the girl to leave with her brother.

l: return with riches, The Library, (21) A Gascon version of the old heathen tale is enriched
s: The boy and girl return to their mother with great riches after escaping from the land of the Ogres. Their wealth comes from the golden horns they collected.

l: The Library, The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: The unit compares the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus with oral and written variants from Sicily, Greece, Albania, Hungary, Syria, and The Arabian Nights. These stories commonly feature travellers trapped by a giant or Cyclops, the blinding of the captor, and escape among sheep or beneath a sheep’s body. The Sicilian, Greek, Albanian, Hungarian, and Arabian versions vary in the number of captives, the giant’s eyes, and the means of escape. Several versions omit either the blinding or the characteristic escape by sheep or sheepskin, while the Syrian tale reverses the usual pattern by restoring the giant’s sight.

l: Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus, The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: The unit treats it as an ancient story type that may survive in oral tradition, especially in Sicily. Its recurring features include a giant’s cave, blinding the giant, and escape among sheep.

l: Ulysses, The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: He is the central human figure of the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus, which the unit compares with later traditional tales.

l: Polyphemus, The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: He is the giant associated with the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus.

l: Sicily, The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: The unit suggests that the story of Ulysses and Polyphemus might survive in oral tradition there. It presents a Sicilian story recorded from an eight-year-old girl and an Albanian version recorded in Sicily.

l: oral tradition, The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: It is presented as a possible means by which the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus has survived, particularly in Sicily.

l: two monks, The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: They lose their way and enter a monster’s cave. The larger monk is killed and roasted, while the other blinds the monster, escapes in a sheep’s skin, and returns to Trapani.

l: small monk, The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: He survives after the monster kills the larger monk. He pretends to eat the roasted flesh, blinds the monster with a heated iron, escapes in a sheep’s skin, and tells fishermen at Trapani what happened.

l: monster (Sicilian cave), The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: He traps two monks in his cave, kills and roasts the larger one, and tries to make the small monk eat him. After being blinded, he releases the sheep, goes fishing, and breaks his head against a rock.

l: cave (Sicilian story), The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: It is the place where the two monks find the monster, are trapped by a great stone, and where the small monk blinds the monster and escapes.

l: Pharasa, The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: It is the place in Cappadocia where a Greek version of the story was recorded.

l: Cappadocia, The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: It is the region associated with the Greek story recorded at Pharasa.

l: Greek story of the seven priests, The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: It tells of seven priests captured by a Cyclops. Six priests blind him with a heated spit, escape in sheep skins, take his sheep, and distribute them among themselves and the wife of the priest who was eaten.

l: seven priests, The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: They form by joining one another during their journey. A Cyclops captures them, eats one, and is then blinded by the other six, who escape disguised in sheep skins.

l: Cyclops (Pharasa story), The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: He seizes seven priests, roasts and eats one, and is blinded when the remaining six drive a heated spit into his eye. He fails to detect them when they escape under sheep skins.

l: Athens, The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: It is the place where another modern Greek version of the story was recorded.

l: prince (Athens story), The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: He enters an Ogre’s cave, eats some of the milk and cake, blinds the sleeping Ogre with a heated stake, and escapes by clinging to the belly of a ram.

l: Ogre (Athens story), The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: He returns to his cave with his sheep, discovers that food is missing, and sleeps. After the prince blinds him, he lets the sheep out by feeling them, while other Ogres mistakenly leave him alone.

l: Psara, The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: It is the island off the west coast of Chios where a version told to Ludwig Ross was recorded.

l: Dimitri, The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: He is one of three brothers who enter a magnificent palace. The blind Ogre seizes him and dashes him to pieces.

l: Michael, The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: He is one of three brothers who enter the Ogre’s palace. The blind Ogre seizes him and dashes him to pieces.

l: George, The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: He escapes the blind Ogre by killing a ram, hiding in its skin, and passing through the gate among the sheep. The Ogre strokes his back but does not recognize him.

l: three brothers, The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: Dimitri, Michael, and George land on an unknown coast and enter a palace containing sheep and a feast. The Ogre kills Dimitri and Michael, while George escapes in a ram’s skin.

l: blind Ogre (Psara story), The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: He appears at the palace, smells human flesh, and kills Dimitri and Michael. He lets George escape because he mistakes him for a ram.

l: Albanian version of the story, The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: It tells of two travellers captured by two Cyclopes with four eyes each. The travellers blind the Cyclopes with heated spits and escape in rams’ skins among the sheep.

l: two travellers (Albanian story), The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: They seek shelter in a cave during a storm and are held there for two days while the Cyclopes fatten them. They blind the Cyclopes and escape by disguising themselves in rams’ skins.

l: two Cyclopes (Albanian story), The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: They have two eyes in front and two behind and try to fatten and eat the two travellers. After being blinded, they guard the cave’s doors and fail to recognize the disguised men among the sheep.

l: rams' skins, The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: They are used by the two travellers in the Albanian story as disguises during their escape from the Cyclopes. Similar sheep skins are used by the six priests in the Pharasa story.

l: Hungarian story of the giant, The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: It concerns three travelling craftsmen who find a one-eyed giant in a sheep stall. After the giant kills Balzer, Laurence and John blind him and escape by passing beneath sheep.

l: Balzer, The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: He is one of three travelling craftsmen in the Hungarian story. The giant identifies him as the fattest, cuts off his head, and gives him to the sheep.

l: Laurence, The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: He is one of the three travelling craftsmen. After the giant is blinded, he escapes by following John’s plan and using an awl while passing through the doorway beneath a sheep.

l: John, The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: He is a shoemaker among the three travelling craftsmen. He blinds the giant with a firebrand and escapes with Laurence by using an awl and passing beneath sheep.

l: three travelling craftsmen, The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: Balzer, Laurence, and John sail for seven days and seven nights before reaching a wood and a sheep stall. The giant kills Balzer, while Laurence and John escape after blinding him.

l: giant (Hungarian story), The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: He has one eye in his forehead and lives in a sheep stall sealed by a great stone. He kills Balzer, is blinded by John, and is later torn to pieces by twelve other giants.

l: modern Syrian version, The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: It tells of a youth who encounters a blind giant in a cave and escapes beneath a he-goat. Unlike the other versions, the youth later recovers and restores the giant’s eyes.

l: Syrian prince, The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: He enters a cave after hearing someone cry and pricks the sleeping giant with a needle. He escapes beneath the belly of a he-goat and later recovers the giant’s lost eyes from a she-bear.

l: blind giant (Syrian story), The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus

l: The Arabian Nights, The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus

l: Third Voyage of Sindibad the Sailor, The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: It tells of Sindibad and companions who encounter a giant that kills and eats several men. They blind him with red-hot spits and escape on rafts, though most are killed by rocks thrown by the giants.

l: Sindibad, The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus

l: giant (Sindibad story), The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: He feels the travellers as a butcher feels sheep, kills and eats three of them over successive days, and sleeps afterward. Sindibad and the others blind him with red-hot spits before escaping.

l: The Story of Seyf El-Mulook, The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: It contains a version in which Saed and memlooks encounter a giant who blinds captives with milk and eats roasted sheep. Saed avoids the milk, blinds the giant with heated spits, and kills him with a sword.

l: Saed, The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: He is shipwrecked with memlooks and reaches a giant’s cave. He avoids being blinded by pretending to drink milk, blinds the giant with heated spits, and cuts him in half with a sword.

l: giant (Seyf El-Mulook story), The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: He keeps blinded men in his cave and blinds new captives by giving them milk. He roasts sheep, is blinded by Saed, and is cut in half with a sword.

l: characteristic escape by sheep or sheepskin, The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: It is a recurring feature in which a captive escapes by hiding under a sheep, clinging to a ram, or wearing a sheep or ram skin. The unit notes that it is absent from both versions in The Arabian Nights and from some other variants.

l: blinding of the giant, The Library, (22) If the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus
s: It is one of the most characteristic incidents of the story type. The giants or Cyclopes are commonly blinded with a heated iron, stake, spit, firebrand, or coal, although the Psara version omits it and the Syrian version restores the giant’s sight instead.

l: The Library, The Library, (32) A story resembling the Homeric tale of Ulysses and
s: The text describes the Armenian popular tale known as the “Story of the Eye in the Forehead,” which resembles the Homeric tale of Ulysses and Polyphemus and has several oral versions. In the Achalzich version, a rich man invites a porter to dinner and tells how, as a merchant and handicraftsman, he survived a shipwreck with twenty companions. A one-eyed giant captured and ate the companions one by one, so the merchant blinded him with a heated iron spit and escaped by boat. The boat was later destroyed by a stone, drowning the others while the merchant survived by tying himself to a board.

l: Story of the Eye in the Forehead, The Library, (32) A story resembling the Homeric tale of Ulysses and
s: The “Story of the Eye in the Forehead” is a widely current Armenian oral tale with several versions. The Achalzich version concerns a one-eyed giant who devours shipwrecked travelers and is blinded by one of them.

l: Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus, The Library, (32) A story resembling the Homeric tale of Ulysses and
s: The Homeric tale of Ulysses and Polyphemus is presented as resembling the Armenian “Story of the Eye in the Forehead.”

l: Armenian popular tale, The Library, (32) A story resembling the Homeric tale of Ulysses and
s: The Armenian popular tale is told orally in Erzerum, Kars, Bajberd, Erzinka, Keghi, and other towns. Armenian emigrants carry it to places including Alexandropol, Achalzich, Achalkalak, and Gumush-chane.

l: rich man, The Library, (32) A story resembling the Homeric tale of Ulysses and
s: The rich man sees a porter carrying a sack of meal, has the sack sent to its destination, and invites the porter to dinner. He tells the porter and the other guests about his own difficult experience.

l: porter, The Library, (32) A story resembling the Homeric tale of Ulysses and
s: The porter complains about his hard and horrible life while resting with a sack of meal. The rich man invites him to dinner and asks him to judge whether his own lot is harder than the experience being recounted.

l: merchant and handicraftsman, The Library, (32) A story resembling the Homeric tale of Ulysses and
s: The narrator identifies himself as a merchant and a handicraftsman who once sailed on business with twenty companions. He survives the shipwreck, the giant's attack, and the destruction of the boat.

l: merchant's twenty companions, The Library, (32) A story resembling the Homeric tale of Ulysses and
s: The merchant's twenty companions are shipwrecked with him and reach the shore. The one-eyed giant eats them one by one, and all are eventually drowned except the merchant.

l: ship, The Library, (32) A story resembling the Homeric tale of Ulysses and
s: The ship carrying the merchant and his twenty companions is overtaken by a great storm, cast onto rocks, and broken into pieces.

l: great storm, The Library, (32) A story resembling the Homeric tale of Ulysses and
s: The great storm overtakes the ship carrying the merchant and his companions. It casts the ship onto rocks and breaks it apart, while the wind carries the travelers ashore.

l: one-eyed giant, The Library, (32) A story resembling the Homeric tale of Ulysses and
s: The one-eyed giant lives in a building in the wood and has an eye in the middle of his forehead. He roasts and eats one of the travelers each evening until the merchant's group blinds him.

l: giant's eye, The Library, (32) A story resembling the Homeric tale of Ulysses and
s: The giant's eye is located in the middle of his forehead. It is pierced and blinded by a red-hot iron spit.

l: iron spit, The Library, (32) A story resembling the Homeric tale of Ulysses and
s: The iron spit is heated in the fire and thrust into the giant's eye on the merchant's advice. The attack blinds the giant and allows the travelers to flee.

l: giant's victims, The Library, (32) A story resembling the Homeric tale of Ulysses and
s: The giant's victims are the merchant's companions. He chooses the strongest and fattest among them, roasts them on a spit, and eats them.

l: giant's cannibal feast, The Library, (32) A story resembling the Homeric tale of Ulysses and
s: The giant's cannibal feast takes place each evening after he returns from walking about. He selects one traveler, roasts him over the fire, and eats him.

l: blinding of the giant, The Library, (32) A story resembling the Homeric tale of Ulysses and
s: The blinding of the giant occurs on the third evening, when one of the travelers thrusts a red-hot spit into his eye. The blinded giant shrieks while the travelers run toward the sea.

l: boat, The Library, (32) A story resembling the Homeric tale of Ulysses and
s: The travelers embark in a boat and row away from the shore after blinding the giant. The giant's mates throw stones at it, and one stone eventually knocks it to pieces.

l: shipwreck and escape, The Library, (32) A story resembling the Homeric tale of Ulysses and
s: The shipwreck leaves the merchant and his companions stranded after their ship breaks on the rocks. After the boat is destroyed and his companions drown, the merchant escapes by tying himself to a board and reaching the shore.

l: The Library, The Library, (33) A version of the tale which presents the main features
s: The unit presents Mingrelian, Ossete, Daghestani, and Oghuz versions of the Homeric story of a one-eyed giant who captures people, devours some of them, is blinded, and is outwitted by escapees disguised in animal skins. In the Mingrelian tale, seven fishermen are captured by a giant after their ship is drawn to a honey stream, and two survivors blind him and escape beneath sheep skins. Urysmag similarly escapes an Ossete giant by burning out his eye and disguising himself as a ram, while a Daghestani mariner uses the same strategy. In the Oghuz tale, Bissat blinds and ultimately kills the invulnerable Depé Ghoz, and the text rejects Wilhelm Grimm’s interpretation of Polyphemus’s eye as the sun.

l: Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus, The Library, (33) A version of the tale which presents the main features
s: The unit compares several Caucasian and Oghuz versions with the Homeric story of a one-eyed giant, the capture and devouring of people, the blinding of the giant, and escape through a flock.

l: traveller (Mingrelian tale), The Library, (33) A version of the tale which presents the main features
s: The traveller is overtaken by night on the road from Redut-Kale to Anaklia and is attacked by wolves. A light leads him to a lonely house, where he hears the host’s account of the seven fishermen.

l: horse (traveller's horse), The Library, (33) A version of the tale which presents the main features
s: The horse stands stock still while wolves attack and cannot be persuaded to move. When a light appears, it gallops toward the lonely house.

l: wolves (forest pack), The Library, (33) A version of the tale which presents the main features
s: The wolves surround the traveller in the forest and try to tear him from his horse. They vanish when a distant light appears.

l: host (lonely house), The Library, (33) A version of the tale which presents the main features
s: The host shelters the traveller in his hut and tells him that his own experiences were worse. He relates how seven fisherman brothers were captured by a one-eyed giant.

l: seven brothers (Mingrelian fishermen), The Library, (33) A version of the tale which presents the main features
s: The seven brothers are fishermen who are captured by a one-eyed giant after being drawn to a honey stream. The giant eats five of them, while two survive by blinding him and escaping in sheep skins.

l: fishermen (Mingrelian brothers), The Library, (33) A version of the tale which presents the main features
s: The fishermen spend months at sea and are towed by a giant fish to a rocky shore. A one-eyed giant later captures them, devours most of them, and is blinded by the surviving brothers.

l: ship (Mingrelian fishermen), The Library, (33) A version of the tale which presents the main features
s: The ship is mysteriously pulled away from shore by a giant fish caught on the fishermen’s hooks. After the fishermen escape the giant, they return home in the ship with selected animals from the giant’s flock.

l: giant fish (Mingrelian tale), The Library, (33) A version of the tale which presents the main features
s: The giant fish has a mouth a fathom wide and greedily drinks the honey flowing into the sea. Its gills hold the fishermen’s hooks, causing it to tow their ship until they cut their lines.

l: honey stream (Mingrelian tale), The Library, (33) A version of the tale which presents the main features
s: The honey stream flows from a rocky shore into the sea. The giant fish drinks from it, and the fishermen load their ship with honey and wax.

l: one-eyed giant (Mingrelian tale), The Library, (33) A version of the tale which presents the main features
s: The giant tends sheep and goats, captures the fishermen, and keeps them in a huge stone building. He roasts and eats them, but the surviving brothers thrust a red-hot spit into his eye and escape beneath sheep skins.

l: giant's flock (Mingrelian tale), The Library, (33) A version of the tale which presents the main features
s: The flock consists of sheep and goats kept in separate compartments of the giant’s building. The surviving fishermen disguise themselves in sheep skins, then select animals and take them aboard their ship.

l: giant's stone building, The Library, (33) A version of the tale which presents the main features
s: The building is made of huge, unhewn blocks of stone and contains separate rooms for goats, sheep, lambs, and kids. The giant shuts the fishermen inside it.

l: roasting spit (Mingrelian tale), The Library, (33) A version of the tale which presents the main features
s: The giant uses the spit to roast animals and captured fishermen. Two surviving brothers pull it from the ground, heat it red-hot, and thrust it into the giant’s eye.

l: Mingrelian fishermen's youngest surviving brother, The Library, (33) A version of the tale which presents the main features
s: He is one of the last two surviving fishermen. He helps blind the giant, disguises himself in a sheep skin, escapes from the building, and reaches the ship.

l: Ossetes, The Library, (33) A version of the tale which presents the main features
s: The Ossetes are described as a Caucasian people who speak an Iranian tongue. Their version features Urysmag and a one-eyed giant.

l: Urysmag, The Library, (33) A version of the tale which presents the main features
s: Urysmag is seized by an Ossete one-eyed giant and placed on a roasting spit. Because the spit passes between his body and clothes, he frees himself, blinds the giant with it, kills the giant’s son, and escapes disguised in the skin of a ram.

l: shipwrecked mariners (Daghestan tale), The Library, (33) A version of the tale which presents the main features
s: Two shipwrecked mariners encounter a one-eyed giant tending sheep. The giant devours one, while the other blinds him with a red-hot iron bar, escapes in a ram’s skin, and reaches the shore on part of the wreck.

l: Oghuz, The Library, (33) A version of the tale which presents the main features
s: The Oghuz are presented as a widely spread branch of the Turkish family, including the Turcomans and the Uzbegs of Bokhara. In the Oghuz narrative, the monster Depé Ghoz preys upon them until Bissat undertakes to kill him.

l: Depé Ghoz, The Library, (33) A version of the tale which presents the main features
s: Depé Ghoz is a semi-divine, one-eyed monster who is invulnerable because of a ring given to him by his fairy mother. He captures Bissat, but Bissat blinds him with a red-hot knife, escapes in a ram’s skin, and finally cuts off his head.

l: Bissat, The Library, (33) A version of the tale which presents the main features
s: Bissat sets out to save the Oghuz and avenge his brother, who was killed by Depé Ghoz. He escapes from the giant’s ox-hide boot, blinds him, gets out disguised in a ram’s skin, and ultimately kills him.

l: ox-hide boot (Depé Ghoz's boot), The Library, (33) A version of the tale which presents the main features
s: Depé Ghoz places Bissat inside his ox-hide boot so that he can roast him later. Bissat cuts the hide with a knife and steps out while the giant sleeps.

l: ring of invulnerability, The Library, (33) A version of the tale which presents the main features
s: The ring is said to make its wearer immune to arrows and swords. Depé Ghoz’s fairy mother gives it to him, and later Depé Ghoz offers it to Bissat, but it falls beneath the giant’s feet when Bissat is attacked.

l: Polyphemus, The Library, (33) A version of the tale which presents the main features
s: Polyphemus is treated as a fairyland one-eyed giant whose story has parallels in the regional tales discussed. The text rejects interpretations that identify him and his fellows with physical or moral principles.

l: eye of Polyphemus, The Library, (33) A version of the tale which presents the main features
s: Wilhelm Grimm interpreted the eye of Polyphemus as the sun. The text dismisses this interpretation as erroneous and treats the eye instead as part of the imaginative construction of a fairyland giant.

l: The Library, The Library, notes
s: This unit is an index of mythological figures, places, objects, and events from Greek mythology. It covers entries from Cadmea and Cadmus through Cyzicus, including stories involving Thebes, Hercules, the Argonauts, Troy, and Odysseus. The entries describe genealogies, marriages, battles, transformations, deaths, voyages, and settlements. No specific entities were provided for individual running-record cells.

l: The Library, The Library, Daedalus makes a statue of Her-
s: Daedalus is an architect and inventor who murders Talos, flees to Minos, constructs the labyrinth, and later escapes from it with wings. Danae, daughter of Acrisius, conceives Perseus by Zeus, is cast into the sea with him, and returns to Argos. Danaus, son of Belus, flees to Argos with his fifty daughters, whose husbands they murder, and later gives them to the winners of an athletic contest. Dionysus, son of Zeus and Semele, discovers the vine, undergoes persecution and madness, spreads his rites, and is recognized as a god.

l: Daedalus, The Library, Daedalus makes a statue of Her-
s: Daedalus makes a statue of Hercules at Pisa and is an architect who is banished from Athens for murder. He makes an artificial cow for Pasiphae, murders his nephew Talos, flees to Minos, constructs the labyrinth, and is shut up in it by Minos. He makes wings for himself, flies to Camicus in Sicily, and is pursued and detected by Minos.

l: Danae, The Library, Daedalus makes a statue of Her-
s: Danae is the daughter of Acrisius. She is shut up in a brazen chamber, conceives Perseus by Zeus, and is cast into the sea with him, drifting to Seriphus. She is loved by Polydectes and later returns with Perseus to Argos.

l: Danaus, The Library, Daedalus makes a statue of Her-
s: Danaus is the son of Belus and settles in Libya, where he has fifty daughters and is said to be the first to build a ship. He flees with his daughters to Argos and obtains the kingdom, then consents to their marriages with the sons of Egyptus; his daughters murder their husbands. He gives his daughters to the victors in an athletic contest.

l: Dionysus, The Library, Daedalus makes a statue of Her-
s: Dionysus is the offspring of Zeus and Semele; he is sewn into his father's thigh, entrusted to Hermes, reared as a girl by Athamas and Ino, and later brought to the nymphs at Nysa. He discovers the vine, is driven mad by Hera, travels through Egypt, Syria, Thrace, India, Thebes, Argos, and other places, spreads his rites, and is recognized as a god. He brings his mother up from Hades and ascends with her to heaven, later comes to Attica, is received by Icarius, and carries off Ariadne from Naxos to Lemnos.

l: The Library, The Library, Erysichthon, son of Cecrops by
s: The unit records mythological figures and events from Erysichthon through Hephaestus. It describes the deeds, deaths, relationships, and genealogies of figures including Hercules, Eumolpus, Eurystheus, Hector, Helen, and Hephaestus. It also records episodes from the Theban conflict, the Trojan War, the Argonautic expedition, and the labours of Hercules.

l: Hercules, The Library, Erysichthon, son of Cecrops by
s: Hercules kills Eryx, Eurition, Eurytion the herdsman of Geryon, Eurytus and Cteatus, Eurytus son of Hippocoon, and Eunomus. He performs labours ordered by Eurystheus, including killing the hydra, pursuing the Stymphalian birds, bringing the Cretan bull, the mares of Diomedes, the belt of Hippolyte, the kine of Geryon, and the apples of the Hesperides. He also cleanses and initiates Eumolpus at Eleusis, crosses the ocean in a golden goblet, wounds Hades, and is carried up to heaven.

l: Eteocles, The Library, Erysichthon, son of Cecrops by
s: Eteocles, son of Oedipus, makes a compact with Polynices to rule alternately. He rules over Thebes, refuses to hand over the kingdom to Polynices, ignores Tydeus's message, puts the Thebans in battle array, and is slain in single combat by Polynices.

l: Polynices, The Library, Erysichthon, son of Cecrops by
s: Polynices makes a compact with Eteocles to rule alternately, but Eteocles refuses to hand over the kingdom of Thebes. Polynices slays Eteocles in single combat.
